learningObjective: Explain FlashAttention's core IO-aware optimization, the mechanism (tiling + online softmax + recomputation), and identify when the speedup is largest.

canonicalClaims.claim: FlashAttention's core IO-optimization is to compute attention block-by-block in SRAM using an online (numerically stable) softmax and to avoid materializing the full N×N attention matrix in HBM; in the backward pass it recomputes intermediates from stored statistics rather than storing the full matrix, so total HBM traffic is reduced from Θ(N²) to Θ(N²·d/M) (where M is SRAM budget).
conditions: The attention block dimensions fit into on-chip SRAM.
The kernel is fused end-to-end so no intermediate goes to HBM.
The softmax is computed incrementally with running-max and running-sum statistics.
nonImplications: Does not imply a change in the attention algorithm's output (up to floating-point ordering).
Does not imply that FlashAttention's speedup is uniform across shapes; it is largest when sequence length N is large enough that HBM traffic for the N×N matrix dominates.

sourceMappings.locator: §3 algorithm and IO analysis; §4 backward with recomputation

canonicalClaims.claim: FlashAttention's speedup versus a naive attention kernel is largest when the sequence length N is large (memory-bound regime), and it can be smaller — or negative once launch overhead is included — for very short sequences where the naive kernel is compute-bound on the SM.
conditions: Comparison is against an unfused naive attention baseline.
Sequence length is the primary axis being varied; head dim d is held moderate.
nonImplications: Does not imply FlashAttention is always faster than every attention kernel; specialized library kernels for short sequences may match or beat it.

misconceptions.claim: FlashAttention changes the attention algorithm's outputs to gain speed (approximate attention).
misconceptions.whyWrong: FlashAttention is exact attention (up to floating-point ordering); it does not approximate.

misconceptions.claim: FlashAttention's core speedup comes from switching to Tensor Cores; without Tensor Cores there would be no benefit over naive attention.
misconceptions.whyWrong: The speedup is from HBM-traffic reduction via tiling and online softmax; Tensor Cores affect FLOP throughput but not the IO cost that FlashAttention primarily eliminates.

misconceptions.claim: FlashAttention gives the same ~2–4× speedup at any sequence length on any GPU; the numbers reported in the paper are hardware-independent constants.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Speedup magnitude depends on shape (large N, moderate d) and hardware (SRAM size, HBM bandwidth, launch overhead); the paper reports specific measurements on specific GPUs.

misconceptions.claim: FlashAttention's advantage in the backward pass comes from storing the entire N×N attention matrix during forward and reusing it during backward.
misconceptions.whyWrong: The paper deliberately does NOT store the N×N matrix; the backward pass recomputes from stored per-row softmax statistics (running-max and running-sum), which is why total memory is Θ(N).
